newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines projects 7.8 pct growth for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Philippines projects 7.8 pct growth for 1997.

text.p: The Philippines on Wednesday projected its economy would grow by 7.8 percent in 1997 and invited Canadian businessmen to invest more in the country, as both sides agreed that bilateral trade was low.

"Being hard-nosed businessmen that you all are, I shall not repeat here all the talk about our being the newest Asian tiger...," President Fidel Ramos told Team Canada, the 350-strong delegation that arrived in Manila on Tuesday to explore business opportunities.

Citing the country's growth figures since 1992, when growth was stagnant, Ramos said: "These are not mere incremental changes over those of the previous years...they show for the very first time that the Philippine economy's growth is sustainable."
Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said the country had set a Gross National Product growth target of 7.8 percent for 1997.
The Philippines has not announced GNP growth for 1996, but has said it will be above the 7.1 percent annualised growth recorded in the first three quarters of the year.
Inflation would be capped within 6.5 percent, down from 8.4 percent in 1996 and 8.1 percent in 1995, he said.

The delegation, headed by Prime Minister Jean Chretien, covers a wide variety of businesses including engineering construction firms, wheat traders, aircraft manufacturers, telecommunications equipment makers and education companies.
Despite the size of the Canadian delegation and talk of the good relations between the two countries, delegates and government officials said business had so far been slow.
At a ceremony on Wednesday, the Canadians signed deals worth $36 million and memoranda of understanding and letters of intent worth $469 million.
But the Canadians, who earlier visited Seoul and were to go to Bangkok as part of a three-nation tour, said the Philippine leg promised the best long-term returns.
"Right now, our business here I shall say is modest. But we see really big growth opporunities," said Michael C. Novak, president of SNC-Lavalin International, an engineering construction firm.
Ramos said that among the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Philippine's share of the Canadian market was the smallest.

Of Canada's total 1995 imports from ASEAN worth $3.98 billion, about 31 percent came from Malaysia, 26 percent from Singapore, 20 percent from Thailand, 12 percent from Indonesia and only 10 percent from the Philippines, he said.
Canadian investment in the Philippines was erratic, Ramos said, citing a high of 1.1 billion pesos ($42 million) in 1990.
"But 1996 was disappointingly low at 1.3 million pesos, or about $50,000," he said.
Chretien in his reply said he hoped the situation would be reversed as "we raise awareness among Canadians of the importance of the Asia-Pacific (region) in our economic lives".
"Even if you expressed disappointment...this visit will mean a new start," he said.
